title: Tenali Raman Tale 97

full_text:
A greedy and heartless sweetmeat vendor named Halwai Ramu operated a grand confectionery shop in the busiest market of Vijayanagara, frying delicious jalebis, gulab jamuns, and ghee laddus in giant copper vats.
A penniless, starving orphan boy named Somu, who had not eaten for two days, stood outside the shop window on the dusty street, inhaling the sweet, fragrant aromas of melting sugar and cardamom wafting from the vats.

The cruel vendor noticed the boy standing there. He grabbed the orphan by his collar, dragged him into the street, and shouted:
'Pay me two silver coins this instant!'
The weeping boy cried: 'Master, I touched nothing! I have no money!'
The vendor yelled: 'Thou hast stood outside my shop for an hour, sniffing the sweet fragrance of my royal jalebis! The aroma of my sweets belongs to me! Pay for the smell, or go to the debtor’s dungeon!'

A crowd gathered, outraged by the vendor's cruelty.
Tenali Raman stepped out from the crowd:
'Release the boy, Halwai Ramu. The boy’s debt shall be paid in full before the entire marketplace!'

Tenali reached into his purse, took out ten bright silver coins, and placed them inside an empty brass water vessel.
Tenali held the brass pot close to the vendor’s right ear.
With a vigorous, rhythmic motion, Tenali shook the pot:
*‘JINGLE-CLINK-CLATTER! JINGLE-CLINK-CLATTER!’*

The coins bounced and chimed loudly inside the brass pot.
Tenali stopped, looked at the vendor, and asked:
'Didst thou hear that sound, Halwai Ramu?'
The vendor blinked: 'Yes, I heard the jingle of ten silver coins!'
Tenali asked: 'Was it a sweet, pleasant sound?'
The vendor nodded greedily: 'Very sweet!'

Tenali smiled with razor-sharp justice:
'Splendid! The account is settled in full!
The poor orphan boy enjoyed the **smell** of thy sweetmeats; and thou hast enjoyed the **sound** of my silver coins!
Neither did he eat thy sweets, nor shalt thou touch my money!
The smell has been paid for with the sound!
Now, take thy hands off the child, or I will have the Market Overseer inspect the quality of thy rancid ghee!'

The entire marketplace roared with triumphant cheers and laughter!
The vendor shrank back into his shop in utter humiliation.
Tenali bought a large box of fresh laddus, handed them to the hungry orphan boy along with two silver coins, proving that poetic justice turns greed into public laughter.
moral: Those who demand payment for the fragrance of food must be paid with the sound of money.
